about: CK-M, the Modeler checkpoint: the two briefs and the supplied model of part B, for readers who work outside Python. No tasks, answers or solutions: those are on the checkpoint page. The water brief and all costs are illustrative; the three days are real 2025 SPP shapes (EIA-930), scaled as the page says.

brief.text: Prairie Town's water utility pumps groundwater into a water tower, and the town draws its water from the tower. Find tomorrow's pumping schedule that meets the town's water use at the least electricity cost for the day.
facts: Water use
forecast for each hour of tomorrow, in the table below (m³)
Pumps
lift up to 900 m³ an hour and use 0.5 kWh of electricity per m³ pumped
Tower
holds 800 to 4,000 m³; 2,000 m³ at the start of the day, and at least as much at the end
Energy price
the rural electric co-op's time-of-use price: $0.06 per kWh from 22:00 to 06:00, $0.20 from 16:00 to 21:00, $0.10 otherwise
Demand charge
$0.40 for each kW of the day's highest hourly draw
brief.note: All numbers in this brief are illustrative.

empirical.text: Prairie Town's planners want to know how far its wind and solar farms can be counted on when the town needs power most. Report what the town can and cannot count on, and how far your results depend on the dataset's scaling.
facts: Data
town_year.json, the course's year file: the real 2025 hourly demand, wind and solar of the Southwest Power Pool grid (EIA-930), each as a shape in thousandths of its own highest 2025 hour
Metadata
the file's meta block gives the source, the time convention and how bad hours were filled
Scaling
as lesson 0: demand × 450 MW, the wind farm × 150 MW, the solar farm × 200 MW, so SPP's highest hour means a farm at its full size
Compare
each farm's output in the 100 hours of highest demand, and in the 100 hours of highest net load (demand minus wind and solar), with its average over the year
Ties
where hours tie, take the earlier one first

sppWind.about: Southwest Power Pool (balancing authority SWPP) operating wind capacity from EIA's monthly generator inventory: units with Status (OP) Operating and Technology Onshore Wind Turbine, nameplate MW summed. The year's average weights each unit by the share of 2025 it was in service, from its operating month; no SWPP wind unit retired in 2025. A like-for-like capacity factor also needs SPP's 2025 wind output in MWh (EIA-930), which the course data hold only as a shape.

defect.about: The supplied model: what should Prairie Town build (wind, solar, a gas combined-cycle plant, a gas peaker) to meet demand on three representative days of 2025, each weighted by the days of the year it stands for? One planted defect.
notes: illustrative round numbers: capital already annualized ($ per MW of capacity per year); running costs as in lesson 0
the three real days' SPP shape × 450 MW
output per MW built: the SPP shapes scaled to EIA's 2025 U.S. capacity factors (33.8% and 24.0%) with the course's scale method
paper: w_d = the days of the year that day d stands for (121, 122, 122; they sum to 365).
min Σ_g A_g K_g + Σ_d w_d Σ_t [ (Σ_g c_g p_g,d,t) + V u_d,t ]   ($ a year)
Σ_g p_g,d,t + u_d,t = D_d,t   (MW, every day and hour)
p_g,d,t ≤ a_g,d,t K_g   (a: output per MW built, 0 to 1)
symbols: a technology: wind, solar, gas combined-cycle (cc), gas peaker (pk)
a representative day, and an hour of it (t = 0 to 23, one hour each)
the days of the year that day d stands for
$ per MW of capacity per year
output in hour t of day d: a decision
MW (held for one hour, so also MWh)
output per MW built, 0 to 1 (wind and solar)
code: DAYS = {"winter": 121, "shoulder": 122, "summer": 122}       # days of 2025 each day stands for
weight = {d: DAYS[d] / 365 for d in DAYS}                    # share of the year
V = 10_000                                                    # $ per MWh of demand left unserved
minimize( sum(capital[g] * K[g] for g) + sum(weight[d] * (sum(cost[g] * p[g,d,t] for g) + V * u[d,t]) for d, t) )
for d, t: sum(p[g,d,t] for g) + u[d,t] == demand[d][t]                 # balance, MW
for g in ("wind", "solar"), d, t: p[g,d,t] <= avail[g][d][t] * K[g]   # output per MW built
for g in ("cc", "pk"), d, t: p[g,d,t] <= K[g]
report(K, annual_cost=objective, demand_in_year=sum(weight[d] * demand[d][t] for d, t))
